sources: WALS Online (Dryer & Haspelmath 2013), CC BY 4.0 — https://wals.info; CLDF dataset cldf-datasets/wals
Li & Thompson (1976), Subject and topic: a new typology of language (topic prominence)
Talmy (2000), Toward a Cognitive Semantics, vol. 2; Slobin (2004) on verb-framed, satellite-framed and equipollent motion encoding
Majid, Bowerman, van Staden & Boster (2007), The semantic categories of cutting and breaking events
Berlin & Kay (1969), Basic Color Terms; Kay, Berlin, Maffi, Merrifield & Cook (2009), The World Color Survey
Haspelmath & König (eds.) (1995), Converbs in Cross-Linguistic Perspective
Daniels & Bright (eds.) (1996), The World's Writing Systems
Reference grammars of the individual languages, listed in languages.json

features.title: Writing system type
features.question: What does one basic sign of the standard script stand for?

values.title: alphabet: letters for consonants and vowels
abjad: letters for consonants, short vowels usually unwritten
abugida: consonant letters with vowel signs attached
logographic: one character per morpheme / syllable
mixed: logograms together with syllabic signs

features.learnerNote: A learner coming from a different script type must learn not only new shapes but a new idea of what a sign stands for, e.g. reading words without vowels or memorising characters that do not spell sounds.

features.title: Writing direction
features.question: In which direction is the standard script written?

values.title: left to right, or in vertical columns (top to bottom, right to left)

features.learnerNote: A learner used to the other direction must retrain eye movement and page layout, including where a book starts and how numbers and foreign words are embedded.

features.title: Letter case
features.question: Does the script have capital and small letters, and which words take a capital?

values.title: capitals for sentence starts and names

features.learnerNote: A learner from a script without case must learn two shapes per letter and the capitalisation rules; one from a case script must learn to recognise names without capitals.

features.title: Vowels in writing
features.question: How are vowels shown in the ordinary written text?

values.title: every vowel is written as a letter
vowel signs attached to consonant letters (abugida), one vowel implied
characters do not spell the sounds (vowels not shown)

features.learnerNote: A learner used to fully written vowels must learn to supply vowels from knowledge of the word (abjad) or to read vowel signs placed around a consonant (abugida); one from a logographic script must learn to spell out sounds.

features.title: Letter shapes by position
features.question: Do letters change their shape depending on their position in the word?

values.title: a few letters have a special word-final shape
letters join and most change shape by position (initial, medial, final, isolated)

features.learnerNote: A learner from a script with fixed shapes must learn up to four forms of each letter and the joining rules; final forms must be learned as a spelling rule.

features.title: Number of scripts
features.question: Is the language written in one script, or in several?

values.title: one script with two standard variants (e.g. simplified / traditional characters)
two different scripts in standard use (by country or region)
several scripts mixed in every text

features.learnerNote: A learner from a one-script language must expect to learn a second character set for full literacy, or to read several scripts side by side in one sentence.

features.title: Spaces between words
features.question: What does the writing separate with spaces or marks?

values.title: no word separation (spaces only between phrases or sentences, if at all)

features.learnerNote: A learner used to word spaces must learn to find word boundaries by knowledge of the vocabulary; one used to unspaced text must learn where the spaces go when writing.

features.title: Stress in writing
features.question: Is the place of word stress shown in the ordinary spelling?

values.title: stress is fixed, predictable or not distinctive
stress is free but never written
an accent mark only where stress breaks the default rule
every word of two or more syllables carries a stress mark

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn the stress of each word with the word itself where it is unmarked, and must learn the accent-mark rules where it is marked.

features.title: Tone in writing
features.question: If the language has tones or a pitch accent, how does the writing show them?

values.title: tone follows from letter classes and tone marks in the syllable spelling
characters do not show tone (romanisations add marks)

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn the tone of each word separately where it is not written, or decode tone from the spelling rules where it is.

features.title: Lexical tone
features.question: Does the pitch of a syllable distinguish words?

values.title: pitch accent: one pitch or accent pattern per word distinguishes some words

features.learnerNote: A learner without tones must hear and produce pitch as part of every word; a learner with tones must learn that here pitch carries only intonation and emotion, not word meaning.

features.title: Word stress
features.question: Where does word stress fall?

values.title: fixed on the last syllable (with few exceptions)
predictable from syllable weight (long vowels, closed syllables)
free: the stressed syllable must be learned with each word
no distinctive word stress (prominence by tone, pitch or phrase)

features.learnerNote: A learner from a fixed-stress language must learn the stress of every word where it is free; a learner from a free-stress language must stop stressing syllables the target language does not.

features.title: Vowel length
features.question: Does the length of a vowel distinguish words?
features.learnerNote: A learner without vowel length must hear and hold long vowels, since a short vowel can make a different word.

features.title: Vowel harmony
features.question: Must the vowels of suffixes match the vowels of the stem?

values.title: nasal harmony: nasality spreads through the word

features.learnerNote: A learner without vowel harmony must learn two or four forms of every suffix and choose them from the stem's vowels.

features.title: Voicing contrast
features.question: Do voiced and voiceless obstruents (b / p, z / s) distinguish words?
features.learnerNote: A learner whose language does not contrast voicing must learn to hear and produce b / p, d / t, z / s as different sounds; a learner with voicing must learn that here another feature (e.g. aspiration) does that job.

features.title: Uvular consonants
features.question: Are there consonants made at the uvula (q, χ, ʁ)?
features.learnerNote: A learner without uvulars must learn to produce sounds further back than k and to keep them apart from k and h.

features.title: Pharyngeal and pharyngealised consonants
features.question: Are there pharyngeal consonants (ħ, ʕ) or pharyngealised 'emphatic' consonants (ṣ, ṭ, ḍ, ẓ)?

values.title: pharyngeals and a series of emphatic consonants

features.learnerNote: A learner without them must learn to produce sounds in the throat and to keep emphatic consonants (which also colour the vowels) apart from plain ones.

features.title: Ejectives and implosives
features.question: Are there glottalised consonants: ejectives (p', t', k') or implosives (ɓ, ɗ)?
features.learnerNote: A learner without them must learn to make consonants with the glottis closed (ejectives) or with an inward airstream (implosives) and to keep them apart from plain consonants.

features.title: Click consonants
features.question: Are clicks used as ordinary consonants?

values.title: yes: clicks are consonants of the language

features.learnerNote: A learner without clicks must learn to produce them inside words, at normal speed, and to distinguish their series.

features.title: Retroflex consonants
features.question: Are there retroflex consonants (tongue tip curled back) that contrast with dental / alveolar ones?

values.title: only as variants (e.g. from r + t)
retroflex sibilants / affricates (ʂ, ʈʂ) contrasting with s-like sounds
retroflex stops (ʈ, ɖ) contrasting with t, d

features.learnerNote: A learner without retroflexes must learn to hear and make a second t / d or s series with the tongue tip curled back.

features.title: Aspiration contrast
features.question: Does aspiration (a puff of air: pʰ vs p) distinguish words?

values.title: four series: voiceless, aspirated, voiced, breathy-voiced

features.learnerNote: A learner whose language does not contrast aspiration must learn that p and pʰ are different sounds that change the word.

features.title: Front rounded vowels
features.question: Are there front rounded vowels (ü / y, ö / ø)?
features.learnerNote: A learner without them must learn to round the lips while saying i or e, and to keep ü apart from u and i.

features.title: Nasal vowels
features.question: Do nasal vowels contrast with oral vowels?
features.learnerNote: A learner without nasal vowels must learn to let air through the nose on the vowel itself, without pronouncing a full n or m.

features.title: Syllable structure
features.question: How complex can syllables be (consonant clusters at the start and end)?

values.title: moderately complex: CCVC with simple clusters

features.learnerNote: A learner from a language with simple syllables must learn to pronounce clusters without inserting extra vowels; one from a cluster language must learn to keep open syllables open.

features.title: Final devoicing
features.question: Do voiced obstruents become voiceless at the end of a word (written d, said t)?

values.title: not applicable: no voicing contrast in obstruents

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn to read a written final b / d / g as p / t / k where devoicing applies, or to keep final voicing where it does not.

features.title: Long (double) consonants
features.question: Does a long (geminate) consonant distinguish words (it. fato / fatto)?
features.learnerNote: A learner without geminates must learn to hold a consonant longer, because a short one can make a different word.

features.title: 'Th' sounds
features.question: Are there interdental fricatives (θ as in 'thin', ð as in 'this')?
features.learnerNote: A learner without θ / ð must learn to put the tongue between the teeth and not replace these sounds with t, s, d or z.

features.title: r and l
features.question: Are r-sounds and l-sounds different phonemes, and are there several r-sounds?

values.title: one liquid: r and l are not distinguished
r and l, and two or more contrasting r-sounds (tap / trill)

features.learnerNote: A learner with a single liquid must learn to keep r and l apart; one with a single r must learn to distinguish tap and trill.

features.title: Hard and soft consonants
features.question: Do consonants come in plain and palatalised ('soft') pairs that distinguish words?
features.learnerNote: A learner without palatalisation must hear and produce soft consonants (with a y-like tongue position) as different sounds and learn how the spelling marks them.

features.title: Unstressed vowel reduction
features.question: Do vowels change quality or disappear when unstressed?

values.title: strong: many unstressed vowels merge into a few weak vowels

features.learnerNote: A learner whose vowels keep their quality must learn that spelling and pronunciation diverge in unstressed syllables and that the stress decides how a vowel sounds.

features.title: Consonant mutation and gradation
features.question: Do consonants at the start or inside a word change because of grammar?

values.title: initial consonant mutation (the first consonant changes after certain words)
consonant gradation (stem consonants alternate between a strong and weak grade)

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn to recognise a word under several initial or internal consonants and to apply the triggering rules when speaking.

features.title: Morphological type
features.question: Which morphological type dominates the language?

values.title: isolating: words do not change; grammar by separate words and order
agglutinating: chains of affixes, one meaning per affix
fusional: endings that carry several meanings at once, stem changes
polysynthetic: one long verb word can express a whole sentence

features.learnerNote: A learner from another type must change how they think of a word: isolating languages need word order and particles, agglutinating ones long suffix chains, fusional ones paradigm tables, polysynthetic ones whole sentences built inside the verb.

features.title: Degree of fusion
features.question: How tightly are grammatical meanings packed into words (the detail behind the morphological type)?

values.title: mostly isolating, with some derivational or voice affixes but no inflection for case, person or tense
agglutinating, with notable fusion and stem alternations
fusional endings, but few of them; much grammar by word order and auxiliaries
fusional: rich paradigms of portmanteau endings
polysynthetic: many morphemes per word, incorporation

features.learnerNote: A learner must adjust the size of the unit they memorise: whole inflected forms in fusional languages, affix by affix in agglutinating ones, separate words in isolating ones.

features.title: Prefixing vs suffixing
features.question: Is inflection mainly expressed by prefixes or by suffixes?
features.learnerNote: A learner from a suffixing language must learn to look at the beginning of the word for grammar (and vice versa), and to find the stem behind the affixes.

features.title: Root-and-pattern morphology
features.question: Are words built by putting vowel patterns into consonantal roots (k-t-b → kataba, kitāb, maktab)?
features.learnerNote: A learner must learn to see the consonantal root behind a word and to read meanings off its pattern, and to look words up by root.

features.title: Stem changes
features.question: Do stems change inside (vowel alternation, ablaut, umlaut, consonant alternation) to mark grammar?

values.title: in part of the vocabulary (irregular verbs, some plurals)
pervasive: a main way of inflecting

features.learnerNote: A learner from a language with invariable stems must learn several stems for one word and the rules or lists that govern them.

features.title: Reduplication
features.question: Is (full or partial) repetition of a word or syllable a productive grammatical process?
features.learnerNote: A learner without reduplication must learn that repeating a word or its first syllable changes its meaning (plural, intensity, repetition, aspect).

features.title: Compounding
features.question: How freely are words joined into compound words?

values.title: restricted: new concepts mostly by phrases (N of N) or derivation
common: noun + noun compounds are frequent
pervasive: the main way of forming words; long compounds

features.learnerNote: A learner from a compounding language must learn to express concepts as phrases with prepositions, and one from a phrasal language must learn to build and take apart long compounds.

features.title: Noun incorporation
features.question: Can a noun (usually the object) be built into the verb word?
features.learnerNote: A learner without incorporation must learn to recognise an object noun inside a verb word and to build such verbs.

features.title: Plural marking on nouns
features.question: Is plurality marked on nouns, and is it obligatory?

values.title: obligatory for human / animate nouns, optional otherwise

features.learnerNote: A learner whose language marks plural optionally must learn to mark it every time; one with obligatory plural must learn to leave nouns unmarked and read number from context.

features.title: Nouns after numerals
features.question: Which form does a noun take after a numeral ('two books')?

values.title: a special form or case depending on the numeral (e.g. genitive, partitive, dual)

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn the noun form each numeral demands: some languages drop the plural after numbers, others require a particular case.

features.title: Dual number
features.question: Is there a grammatical dual (a form for exactly two)?

values.title: only in pronouns or verb forms
on a limited set of nouns (pairs, units of time)

features.learnerNote: A learner without a dual must use a third number form for exactly two things and make other words agree with it.

features.title: Collective and singulative
features.question: Is there a basic collective noun from which a 'single unit' noun is derived (tree(s) → one tree)?
features.learnerNote: A learner must learn that the basic noun can mean the whole mass or class, and that a single item needs a derived (often longer) form.

features.title: Number of genders / noun classes
features.question: How many genders or noun classes control agreement?
features.learnerNote: A learner without gender must learn the gender of every noun as part of the word and make other words agree with it; one with gender must learn to stop marking it.

features.title: Basis of gender
features.question: On what basis are nouns sorted into genders or classes?

values.title: not sex-based (e.g. human / non-human, shape, noun classes)

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn which nouns go into which class; in noun-class languages the class is marked by a prefix and changes in the plural.

features.title: Number of cases
features.question: How many morphological cases do nouns have?
features.learnerNote: A learner without cases must learn to change the noun's ending by its role in the sentence, often together with prepositions; a learner with cases must learn to carry those roles by word order and prepositions.

features.title: Case syncretism
features.question: Do different cases share the same form?

values.title: no syncretism: each case has its own form
only between core cases (e.g. nominative = accusative)
also involving other cases (e.g. genitive = dative)

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn that one ending can stand for several cases and read the role from context, agreement or prepositions.

features.title: How case is marked
features.question: By what means are case relations marked on the noun phrase?

values.title: no case affixes or case clitics

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn where case is shown: at the end of the noun, at its beginning, or in a small word attached to the whole phrase.

features.title: Alignment
features.question: Is the subject of an intransitive verb treated like the agent or like the object of a transitive verb?

values.title: ergative: intransitive subject = transitive object; the agent is marked
split: ergative or active in some tenses / persons, accusative elsewhere
active: depends on whether the subject acts or undergoes
symmetrical voice: a verb voice picks which argument is the pivot
neutral: no case or agreement distinguishes the roles

features.learnerNote: A learner from an accusative language must learn that the 'subject' case can depend on transitivity, tense or voice; ergative languages mark the doer of a transitive verb specially.

features.title: Definite article
features.question: Is there a definite article ('the'), and where does it go?

values.title: a separate word before the noun
a separate word after the noun

features.learnerNote: A learner without articles must learn to decide definiteness in every noun phrase; one with articles must learn to express it by context, word order or demonstratives.

features.title: Indefinite article
features.question: Is there an indefinite article ('a'), and is it the word for 'one'?
features.learnerNote: A learner without an indefinite article must learn when 'a / one' is required; one with an article must learn to leave nouns bare.

features.title: Numeral classifiers
features.question: Must a classifier (measure word) stand between a numeral and a noun ('three CL books')?
features.learnerNote: A learner without classifiers must learn the right classifier with each noun; one with classifiers must learn to count nouns directly.

features.title: Possessive affixes
features.question: Is the possessor ('my', 'your') marked by an affix on the noun?
features.learnerNote: A learner without possessive affixes must learn a set of person endings for nouns ('house-my'); one with them must learn separate possessive words.

features.title: Alienable and inalienable possession
features.question: Does the way of saying 'my X' depend on the kind of thing or relation possessed?

values.title: inalienable (body parts, kin) vs alienable possession
a / o classes chosen by the relation between possessor and possessed

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn which nouns or relations take which possessive construction, e.g. body parts and relatives vs ordinary objects.

features.title: Construct state and linkers
features.question: Does a noun take a special form or a linker when it is followed by a possessor or modifier?

values.title: construct state: the head noun takes a special bound form ('house-of the-man')
ezafe: a linking vowel after the head noun before its modifiers
a linker particle between modifier and noun

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn to change or extend the first noun of a phrase rather than to mark the possessor alone.

features.title: Possessive noun phrase ('the man's house')
features.question: How is a possessor noun linked to the possessed noun?

values.title: an ending or clitic on the possessor (genitive case, 's)
a separate word ('of', 'de', 的, の)
a marker on the possessed noun
the possessed noun takes a construct / bound form
a linker attached to the possessed noun (ezafe type)
the two nouns are simply placed side by side

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn which of the two nouns carries the marking and in which order they come.

features.title: Subject agreement on the verb
features.question: Does the verb change for the subject, and for what?

values.title: person, number and (in some forms) gender

features.learnerNote: A learner without agreement must learn conjugation tables; one with agreement must learn that here the verb stays the same and the subject must be said.

features.title: Object marking on the verb
features.question: Is the object (its person, number or definiteness) marked on the verb?

values.title: unstressed object pronouns attached to or fixed next to the verb
agreement: the verb marks the object even when a full object noun is present
the verb has a separate conjugation for definite objects

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn to mark the object inside the verb word, possibly twice (with a pronoun and a noun), or to stop doing so.

features.title: Obligatory tense
features.question: Must every finite verb (or clause) be marked for tense?

values.title: yes: tense or a tense-aspect marker in every finite clause
an aspect or mood marker is obligatory, but not tense
no: time is shown by optional particles, adverbs or context

features.learnerNote: A learner from a tenseless language must mark time on every verb; a learner with tense must learn to leave time to adverbs and context.

features.title: Past tense
features.question: Is there a grammatical past tense, and does it distinguish degrees of remoteness?

values.title: two or more pasts by remoteness (today / yesterday / long ago)

features.learnerNote: A learner without a past tense must mark every past event on the verb; one with a single past must learn to choose between near and remote pasts.

features.title: Future tense
features.question: How is future time expressed?

values.title: no grammatical future: the present / non-past or optional words

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn whether a future form is required, built with an auxiliary, or left to context.

features.title: Perfective / imperfective aspect
features.question: Does the grammar distinguish completed (perfective) from ongoing / habitual (imperfective) events?

values.title: yes, by verb forms (e.g. aorist vs imperfect)
yes, by pairs of verbs (usually prefix or suffix derived)

features.learnerNote: A learner without aspect must decide for every past or future verb whether the event is seen as a whole or as ongoing; with verb pairs, every verb must be learned twice.

features.title: Progressive
features.question: Is there a progressive ('is doing') form, and must it be used for ongoing events?

values.title: a progressive exists but the simple form also covers ongoing events

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn whether 'I eat' can mean 'I am eating', and when the progressive form is required.

features.title: Perfect
features.question: Is there a perfect ('has done', with present relevance), and what is it built from?
features.learnerNote: A learner must learn when the perfect (rather than a simple past) is required, and how it is built.

features.title: Subjunctive
features.question: Is there a subjunctive (a verb form for wishes, purposes, possibilities in subordinate clauses)?

values.title: yes: a particle (often with special forms), e.g. να, să, да, бы

features.learnerNote: A learner without a subjunctive must learn which conjunctions and verbs trigger it and its forms; one with it must learn to use ordinary forms.

features.title: Conditional
features.question: How is 'would / if' expressed?

values.title: a conditional verb form or conditional suffix
an auxiliary or particle (would, würde, бы, θα)
only a conjunction 'if'; the verb is unchanged

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn whether 'if / would' is carried by a verb form, an auxiliary, or a conjunction alone.

features.title: Optative
features.question: Is there a dedicated inflectional form for wishes ('may he live')?
features.learnerNote: A learner must learn a separate verb form for wishes and blessings, or to express them with 'let' / 'may' constructions.

features.title: Evidentiality
features.question: Must the verb show how the speaker knows the information (seen, inferred, heard)?
features.learnerNote: A learner without evidentials must choose a verb form according to whether they witnessed the event or know it from others or from traces.

features.title: Mirativity
features.question: Is there a grammatical form for new or surprising information ('so he IS here!')?
features.learnerNote: A learner must learn the verb form or particle that signals surprise or newly discovered facts.

features.title: Passive
features.question: Is there a passive, and how is it formed?

values.title: with an auxiliary or particle (be + participle, 被)
with a verb affix or stem pattern
a voice system: any of several arguments can be made the pivot

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn how (and how often) the language promotes the object to subject, or how it avoids doing so.

features.title: Antipassive
features.question: Is there an antipassive (the object is demoted or dropped and the agent becomes an ordinary intransitive subject)?
features.learnerNote: A learner must learn a detransitivising verb form used when the patient is indefinite or unimportant, typical of ergative languages.

features.title: Causative morphology
features.question: Can 'make someone do' be formed by changing the verb itself?

values.title: a productive causative affix or pattern

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn the causative affix and how it changes the case of the person made to act, or to use a separate 'make / let' verb.

features.title: Applicative
features.question: Can a verb affix add a new object (beneficiary, place, instrument): 'cook-for someone'?
features.learnerNote: A learner must learn that a verb affix can turn a beneficiary or location into a direct object.

features.title: Verb particles and preverbs
features.question: Are there verbs with particles or prefixes that change meaning, and do they separate from the verb?

values.title: no systematic class of particle verbs
prefixed verbs whose prefix stays attached
phrasal verbs: a separate particle after the verb
separable: the particle is attached in some forms and detached in others

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn the meaning of each particle verb as a unit and, for separable ones, where the particle goes in each clause type.

features.title: Light-verb compounds
features.question: Are many verbs formed as noun + 'do / make / be' (kar kardan, 勉強する, 공부하다)?

values.title: the main way of forming new verbs

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn verbs as noun + light verb units and which light verb each noun takes.

features.title: Separable verb-object compounds
features.question: Are there verbs made of verb + object that split around other words (睡觉 → 睡了一个好觉)?
features.learnerNote: A learner must learn that such verbs already contain their object and how aspect markers and modifiers are inserted inside them.

features.title: Converbs and clause chaining
features.question: Are there non-finite adverbial verb forms ('having done', 'while doing') used to chain clauses?

values.title: yes, and chaining with converbs is the main way to link clauses

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn to link clauses with a non-finite verb form and leave only the last verb finite, or (the other way round) to use finite verbs joined by 'and'.

features.title: Infinitive
features.question: Is there an infinitive ('to go'), and what replaces it if not?

values.title: a finite subordinate clause or subjunctive instead
not applicable: verbs do not change form

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn to say 'I want to go' as 'I want that I go' (or with a verbal noun) where there is no infinitive, and to master infinitive constructions where there is.

features.title: Participles
features.question: Are there participles (adjectival verb forms), and how many?

values.title: none (or not distinct from finite forms)
one or two, mostly in compound tenses
several, by tense / voice, used like relative clauses

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn to turn a relative clause into a participle phrase ('the book read by me') or vice versa.

features.title: Honorific forms
features.question: Do verbs or words change to show respect for the person spoken about or to?

values.title: no (respect only through pronouns or titles)
special honorific vocabulary (royal, religious or respectful words)
honorific verb morphology and speech levels

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn a second set of words or verb forms for respected people and when to use them.

features.title: Adjectives as verbs
features.question: Does a predicative adjective ('the house is big') behave like a verb?

values.title: verbal: adjectives inflect / predicate like verbs, no copula

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn to use adjectives as verbs (with tense and negation, no 'to be'), or to add a copula.

features.title: Adjective agreement
features.question: Does an attributive adjective agree with its noun, and in what?
features.learnerNote: A learner without agreement must learn the adjective's endings for each noun; one with agreement must learn to leave adjectives unchanged.

features.title: Comparative of adjectives
features.question: Is 'bigger' formed with an affix or with a separate word ('more big')?
features.learnerNote: A learner must learn the comparative endings (and the irregular ones) or to build comparatives with a degree word.

features.title: Basic word order
features.question: What is the dominant order of subject, object and verb?
features.learnerNote: A learner must re-order the sentence around the verb (e.g. put it at the end or the beginning) and rely on case or particles where the order is free.

features.title: Verb-second
features.question: Must the finite verb be the second element of a main clause?

values.title: verb-second in main clauses and verb-final in subordinate clauses

features.learnerNote: A learner must invert subject and verb after any fronted element and, where applicable, send the verb to the end of subordinate clauses.

features.title: Prepositions or postpositions
features.question: Do adpositions come before or after their noun phrase?
features.learnerNote: A learner must learn to put the relational word after the noun ('the house in') or before it.

features.title: Adjective and noun
features.question: Does the adjective come before or after the noun?
features.learnerNote: A learner must reverse the usual order of adjective and noun, and learn any adjectives that keep a special position.

features.title: Possessor and noun
features.question: Does the possessor come before or after the possessed noun?
features.learnerNote: A learner must reverse the order of 'X's Y' / 'Y of X'.

features.title: Numeral and noun
features.question: Does a numeral come before or after the noun?
features.learnerNote: A learner must learn to put the number after the noun (often with a classifier) or before it.

features.title: Demonstrative and noun
features.question: Does 'this / that' come before or after the noun?

values.title: after the noun (or as a suffix)
on both sides of the noun

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn the position of demonstratives, which may differ from that of adjectives and articles.

features.title: Relative clause and noun
features.question: Does a relative clause follow or precede its noun?

values.title: the noun stays inside the relative clause

features.learnerNote: A learner must build relative clauses before the noun (and wait for the noun at the end), or after it.

features.title: How relative clauses are marked
features.question: What marks a relative clause?

values.title: a relative pronoun (who / which / der / который)
an invariant particle or complementiser (που, que, she-, 的)
a special verb form (participle, relative affix)
nothing: the clause is simply placed next to the noun

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn the relative word (and its case / gender forms) or the participle forms that replace relative clauses.

features.title: Subject pronouns
features.question: Can subject pronouns be left out?

values.title: yes: the verb shows the subject, pronouns are for emphasis
yes: pronouns are omitted when clear from context, without agreement
only in some persons or tenses

features.learnerNote: A learner from a pro-drop language must always say the subject; one from a non-pro-drop language must learn to leave it out.

features.title: Copula 'to be' in the present
features.question: Is 'to be' needed in present-tense sentences like 'he is a teacher'?

values.title: no copula in the present (or at all): 'he teacher'
absent in the 3rd person only; 1st / 2nd person take a copula or ending

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn to build sentences without 'is' (nominal sentences) or to always add it.

features.title: 'Is' (identity) vs 'is' (location)
features.question: Are 'X is a teacher' and 'X is at home' expressed with the same word?

values.title: different words (e.g. ser / estar, 是 / 在)

features.learnerNote: A learner must choose between two 'to be' verbs (identity vs location / state) or learn that one covers both.

features.title: Predicative possession ('I have')
features.question: How is 'I have a book' expressed?

values.title: '(as for) me, there is a book' / existential with topic

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn to express possession with an existential and a case or preposition instead of a 'have' verb, or vice versa.

features.title: Yes / no questions
features.question: How are yes / no questions marked?

values.title: a particle exists, but intonation alone is common

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn the question particle and its position, inversion, or that intonation alone suffices.

features.title: Position of the question particle
features.question: Where does the yes / no question particle go?

values.title: no question particle in common use
at the beginning of the clause
after the first word or phrase
at the end of the clause
right after the word being questioned

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn where to put the question particle, which may depend on what is being asked about.

features.title: Question words
features.question: Are question words (who, what, where) moved to the front?

values.title: yes, to the start of the clause
no: they stay in place (or go before the verb)

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn to leave the question word where the answer would stand, or to move it to the front.

features.title: Negation
features.question: How is a sentence negated?

values.title: a negative affix on the verb

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn the negator's form and whether it is a separate word, an affix, a conjugated verb or two parts around the verb.

features.title: Position of negation
features.question: Where does the negator stand relative to the verb?

values.title: after the verb (or as a suffix)
depends on clause type or verb position

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn where the negation goes, which can differ between main and subordinate clauses.

features.title: Negative concord
features.question: With 'nobody / nothing', is the verb also negated ('nobody did not come')?

values.title: yes: the verb is always negated too

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn whether 'nobody' needs an extra 'not' on the verb, since doubling can be required or wrong.

features.title: Topic prominence
features.question: Is the sentence organised around a grammatical subject or around a topic ('as for X, …')?

values.title: both subject and topic are grammatically marked

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn to start with what the sentence is about and comment on it, or to build sentences around a grammatical subject that agrees with the verb.

features.title: Serial verbs
features.question: Can several verbs be strung together in one clause without conjunctions ('take knife cut meat')?
features.learnerNote: A learner must learn to express direction, instrument, result or purpose by chaining bare verbs, or to replace such chains with prepositions and subordinate clauses.

features.title: Switch reference
features.question: Does a dependent verb show whether its subject is the same as that of the main verb?
features.learnerNote: A learner must choose the dependent verb form by whether the subject changes between clauses.

features.title: Subordinate clauses
features.question: Are subordinate clauses mainly finite clauses with conjunctions, or non-finite verb forms (participles, nominalisations, converbs)?

values.title: non-finite verb forms with case endings or postpositions

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn to turn 'because he came' into a nominalised verb with a case ending, or the other way round.

features.title: Position of obliques
features.question: Where do adverbial phrases (place, time, instrument) stand relative to verb and object?

values.title: after verb and object (V O X)
before the verb, object after (X V O)
before object and verb (X O V)
between object and verb (O X V)

features.learnerNote: A learner must move time, place and manner phrases before the verb (e.g. in Chinese) or after the object.

features.title: Comparative construction
features.question: How is 'X is bigger than Y' built?

values.title: with a verb 'exceed / pass' (big pass Y)
by two clauses (X is big, Y is small)

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn the case, preposition or verb that marks the standard of comparison.

features.title: Gender in personal pronouns
features.question: Do personal pronouns distinguish masculine and feminine?

values.title: also in the 1st or 2nd person (e.g. 'you' masc. / fem.)

features.learnerNote: A learner must choose pronouns (and verb forms) by the sex of the person spoken about or to, or learn that one pronoun covers both.

features.title: Inclusive and exclusive 'we'
features.question: Are there two words for 'we': including the listener and excluding them?
features.learnerNote: A learner must decide every time whether 'we' includes the person addressed.

features.title: Politeness in pronouns (T / V)
features.question: Does the choice of 'you' depend on politeness?

values.title: pronouns are avoided; titles and kin terms used instead

features.learnerNote: A learner must choose the form of address (and the matching verb forms) by relationship and situation.

features.title: Speech levels
features.question: Do verb endings or sentence particles change with the formality of the situation?

values.title: two levels of verb endings (plain / polite)
several speech levels in the verb endings

features.learnerNote: A learner must mark the level of politeness in every sentence, choosing endings or particles by the addressee.

features.title: Diglossia
features.question: Is the written / formal standard markedly different from the everyday spoken language?

values.title: a noticeable gap (forms and words differ)
two distinct varieties for formal and everyday use

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn two varieties, or at least two sets of forms, and when each is used.

features.title: Speaker's gender in speech
features.question: Does what a speaker says about themselves change with the speaker's gender?

values.title: yes, by agreement (e.g. 'I was tired' differs for a man and a woman)
yes, by gendered pronouns, particles or kin terms

features.learnerNote: A learner must mark their own gender in verb or adjective forms, or choose gendered particles and pronouns.

features.title: Kinship: uncles
features.question: How are the father's and the mother's brothers named?

values.title: one word for both uncles, distinct from 'father' (English type)
different words for father's brother and mother's brother
father's brother called 'father' (big / small father), mother's brother distinct

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn separate words by the side of the family (and sometimes by relative age), or learn that one word covers several relatives.

features.title: Kinship: older and younger siblings
features.question: Do the basic words for siblings distinguish older and younger?
features.learnerNote: A learner must always know (and say) whether a sibling is older or younger.

features.title: Verbs of knowing
features.question: Are 'know a fact' and 'know a person / be acquainted' different verbs?
features.learnerNote: A learner must choose the verb by what is known (a fact or a person / place), or learn that one verb covers both.

features.title: Verbs of wearing
features.question: Is there one verb for wearing / putting on everything, or several by body part or item?

values.title: several by body part (body, feet, head, hands …)

features.learnerNote: A learner must choose the wearing verb by the item (shirt, shoes, hat, glasses, ring).

features.title: Verbs of carrying
features.question: Is there one basic verb 'carry', or must the manner (in the hand, on the back, on the shoulder, in the arms) be chosen?
features.learnerNote: A learner must choose the carrying verb by how the thing is carried.

features.title: Verbs of cutting
features.question: Is there a general 'cut', or must the instrument (knife vs scissors) be chosen?

values.title: different verbs by instrument (no general verb)

features.learnerNote: A learner must choose the cutting verb by instrument and manner.

features.title: Green and blue
features.question: Are green and blue named by different basic colour words?

values.title: no, one basic word covers both

features.learnerNote: A learner must split (or merge) the colour range, e.g. qualify a single 'grue' word as 'leaf-grue' / 'sky-grue'.

features.title: Motion verbs: manner vs path
features.question: Does the verb usually express the path of motion (enter, exit) or the manner (run, float) with the path in a particle?

values.title: manner in the verb, path in a particle or prefix (run in, hineinlaufen)
both as equal verbs (跑进来: run-enter-come)

features.learnerNote: A learner must re-package motion events: put the direction in the verb and the manner in an adverbial, or the other way round.

features.title: Position verbs
features.question: Is the location of objects normally expressed with posture verbs (the book lies, the glass stands)?

values.title: posture verbs (stand, lie, sit, hang) are the normal way

features.learnerNote: A learner must choose 'stand', 'lie' or 'sit' by the shape and orientation of an object, or learn to use a generic 'be'.

features.title: Numeral base
features.question: What is the base of the counting system?
features.learnerNote: A learner must learn to count in twenties (four-twenty = 80) or with a five-based system for the lower numbers.

features.title: Order of tens and units
features.question: Is 21 said as 'twenty-one' or 'one-and-twenty'?
features.learnerNote: A learner must reverse the order of tens and units when saying or hearing numbers.

features.title: Numeral agreement
features.question: Do numerals change for gender, case or noun class?
features.learnerNote: A learner must inflect numerals with the noun (and, in Arabic, even reverse their gender), or learn that they are invariable.

features.title: Large numbers
features.question: How are large numbers grouped?

values.title: a separate word for each power of ten up to a million

features.learnerNote: A learner must regroup digits when reading large numbers (10,000 = one myriad; 100,000 = one lakh).

features.title: Telling the half hour
features.question: How is 2:30 said?

values.title: another time-reckoning (e.g. hours counted from dawn)

features.learnerNote: A learner must shift the hour when telling the half hour, or learn a different starting point of the day.

features.title: Names of the weekdays
features.question: How are the days of the week named?

values.title: mostly by number (second day, third day …)

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn weekday names as vocabulary where they are not numbered, or use the numbering where they are.

features.title: Names of the months
features.question: How are the months named?
features.learnerNote: A learner must learn twelve native month names where they are not Latin-derived or numbered.

features.title: Calendar in use
features.question: Which calendar is used for dates in everyday life?

values.title: Gregorian, with a traditional calendar for festivals / religious dates
an official non-Gregorian calendar or era count

features.learnerNote: A learner must learn to read dates in another calendar or era, and that festivals move against the Gregorian year.
